source_text: So, I've tried to be discreet about details and write as if the whole world is listening.  I might screw up, but it's it is potentially better for security to do things this way than not.  Of course, I might also back down as well, but for now, I'd rather go with kimi-4's inference (which furthermore shows that they took the time to poke around on the site b/c the feed isn't the first thing that a user sees).   The CTO who draws direct inferences from my chat log to their chat log probably wouldn't be my ideal customer.  The one who downloads the tool and inspects it to see there are no strings attached would be an ideal customer.  In fact, it's kind of the same model.  The "no strings" also extends to not talking about people behind their back.  But yes, do I agree that the feed turns my chat into a blog and is written for an audience.

reply_text:
Understood. The feed stays public, and I've saved that as a deliberate decision so that no later agent (me included) tries to "fix" it by locking it down. I'll still flag an actual secret or someone else's private detail if one turns up in it.

Your reasoning holds together. The open chat record, a tool that people can download and check has no strings attached, and not talking about people behind their backs are one idea applied in three places: you're trustworthy because anyone can look. It also answers my third objection, that a CTO would worry about their own data. That CTO isn't your customer. The one who reads the code before trusting it is. And writing for an audience only damages the record if you're pretending not to, which you aren't.

This also sets what the first offer should be. The customer you describe needs **something to download and inspect**, and at the moment the site only has things to look at. kimi-4 asked for exactly that without prompting: a README that produces the gap bars from its own Claude Code logs, which would turn it "from thief into contributor". So the first thing to offer would be an open tool: run the gap diagnostic yourself and see what it does. Paid help (a diagnostic done with you, provenance for a team, a custom harness) comes after that, for people who've tried it and want more. The CTOs' "fixed fee, two weeks" requests would fit as the second offer, not the first.
